tier_reason: First-party README table on a named CPU (i5-7360U) and toolchain (Go 1.26 darwin/amd64), and the MD5 stdlib row has a public harness (internal/md5x8/bench_test.go TestBenchmarkReport times md5x8 against md5.Sum on a 9-byte message). The README never says which command produced the table, the crypto/sha1 4.1 MH/s row has no harness in the repo (internal/sha1x8/bench_test.go times only the 8-way kernels), and the kernel row times compression of a pre-built constant buffer against a full md5.Sum, so it stays C.

corrections.caveats: A stdlib comparison harness does exist for MD5: internal/md5x8/bench_test.go TestBenchmarkReport times md5x8 on a pre-built transposed buffer (the same 8 candidates every iteration, compression only) against md5.Sum([]byte("cand-0000")), which also pays digest init, padding and finalization, so the 48 vs 5.7 MH/s kernel ratio overstates the per-compression gain; the end-to-end brute-force pipeline (38 MH/s, generator included) is the fairer 1-core figure, about 6.7x (derived from page data). No harness for the crypto/sha1 4.1 MH/s row was found (internal/sha1x8/bench_test.go benchmarks only the sha1x8 digest and match kernels). The README does not say which command produced the table. Go's crypto/md5 and crypto/sha1 on amd64 are themselves scalar assembly, so this is 8-lane multi-buffer AVX2 against single-stream scalar code, not like-for-like latency. Single 2-core laptop, single run, no repeat statistics. No LICENSE file (usability reference). Two commits (both 2026-09-28), one star. Password-cracking tool; README says it is for authorised testing and recovery of credentials you own. Candidates limited to 55 bytes (one block).

notes: All numbers match the README table. The record's claim that no stdlib benchmark harness exists is wrong for MD5 (TestBenchmarkReport in internal/md5x8/bench_test.go) but right for SHA-1. Low notability (1 star, 2 commits, two weeks old); kept at C, reference only (no license).

tier_reason: First-party release notes (NEWS 1.9.0 and 1.12.0) carry every quoted ratio; the linked commit messages add before/after bench-slope figures with CPU models (Celeron J3455 for SHA-NI SHA-1, Ryzen 9 9950X3D for VAES/AVX512 AES) but no compiler or flags, so first-party with partial methodology: C.

corrections.baseline: libgcrypt's own previous implementation of the same primitive, which differs per row: earlier assembly paths for several rows (VAES/AVX512 AES is measured against libgcrypt's VAES/AVX2 assembly; AES-NI XTS against earlier AES-NI code; SHA-NI SHA-1 against the previous SHA-1 path), generic C for others; NEWS does not say which
corrections.claimed_speedup: NEWS 1.9.0 (2021-01-19): Intel SHA extension for SHA-1 and SHA-256 '(4.0/3.7 times faster)'; AES-NI AES-XTS '(6 times faster)'; ARMv8/CE AES-XTS '(2.5 times faster)'; AVX/AVX2 Blake-2 '(1.3/1.4 times faster)'; i386/SSSE3 SHA-512 '(4.5 times faster on Ryzen 7)'; ARMv8/CE PMULL CRC '(7 times faster)'; ARMv7/NEON GCM '(3 times faster)'; CAST5 40-70% and Blowfish 60-80% faster. NEWS 1.12.0 (2026-01-29): VAES/AVX512 AES 'boosts OCB performance by about 2 times on AMD Zen5'. Commit 9e3af928ee: Ryzen 9 9950X3D OCB enc 0.030 to 0.016 ns/B (32298 to 61035 MiB/s) against the VAES/AVX2 path, no change on Zen4. Commit d02958bd30: SHA-1 on Celeron J3455 4.50 to 1.11 ns/B (211.7 to 858.1 MiB/s, '4.0x faster').
corrections.hardware: NEWS: Ryzen 7 (SHA-512 row) and AMD Zen5 (OCB row); commit messages: Intel Celeron J3455 1500 MHz no turbo (SHA-1 SHA-NI, d02958bd30), AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D, Ryzen 9 7900X and Intel Core i3-1115G4 (VAES/AVX512, 9e3af928ee); other rows not checked
corrections.license: LGPL-2.1 (library, COPYING.LIB); GPL-2.0 for helper programs and documentation (COPYING)
corrections.caveats: Release-note claims; the commit messages behind them give bench-slope before/after numbers and CPU models but never compiler or flags. The baseline is libgcrypt's previous code for the same primitive, often already assembly (the Zen5 OCB 2x is VAES/AVX512 against libgcrypt's own VAES/AVX2 assembly, and Zen4/Tigerlake see no gain), not a plain compiler build. Several rows are C with inline assembly or intrinsics (sha1-intel-shaext.c) rather than .S files. The i3-1115G4 table in commit 9e3af928ee has its before/after labels reversed. A correctness fix landed on 2026-10-11 in cipher/poly1305-amd64-avx512.S (lost carry and bit 130 in base 2^44 conversions gave wrong Poly1305 tags), not one of the claimed rows. GitHub repo is a mirror of dev.gnupg.org; maintainers do not track it.

notes: All quoted NEWS figures verified verbatim in NEWS 1.9.0 and 1.12.0; two commit messages checked for underlying numbers. Baseline corrected: several rows compare against libgcrypt's own earlier assembly, not generic C, so baseline_in_list is doubtful for those rows (left unchanged). Note the Poly1305 AVX-512 wrong-tag fix of 2026-10-11 as a quality shortcoming.

tier_reason: First-party go test -bench output in the README from the public blake3_test.go (BenchmarkSum256, BenchmarkWrite, BenchmarkXOF), but no Go version or command is given and the CPU line is self-contradictory, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Sum256 65536 B: 16245 ns (4034 MB/s) AVX-512, 31137 ns (2105 MB/s) AVX2, 133505 ns (491 MB/s) pure Go; about 8.2x for AVX-512 and about 4.3x for AVX2 (derived from page data). Write (1 KiB writes): 245 ns AVX-512, 487 ns AVX2, 2022 ns pure Go (about 8.3x and 4.2x, derived). XOF: 246 ns AVX-512, 329 ns AVX2, 1914 ns pure Go (about 7.8x and 5.8x, derived). No gain for 64 B and 1 KiB inputs (identical figures in all three listings).
corrections.caveats: Author's own run from August 2020 (README benchmark sections were added in commits of 2020-08-01 to 2020-08-10 and not updated since): no Go version or flags, and the CPU line ('2020 MacBook Air (i5-7600K @ 3.80GHz)') is contradictory, since the i5-7600K is a desktop part without AVX-512. The identical 64 B and 1 KiB rows are explained by the code: guts/compress_amd64.go uses the AVX-512/AVX2 paths only for buffers of at least two chunks (2 KiB), and the README says there is no assembly routine for single-block compressions, so small inputs run pure Go in all three builds; identical ns values suggest one run was pasted. Later code differs from the measured version: a goroutine-parallel path (PR #25, 2025) and a split-Write correctness fix (83c0fac, 2025-05-08, with the buggy version retracted). Baseline is the package's own pure-Go path, not a third-party library. The assembly is generated by avo, not hand-written.

notes: All README numbers match; small-input identical rows are by design (SIMD only from 2 KiB). Metadata verified: MIT, 425 stars, last commit 2025-05-08 (stale). The 2020 MacBook Air uses Ice Lake parts with AVX-512, so the i5-7600K string is likely the wrong label (not confirmed on the page).
